title: Agile Online Model Selection: Resolving Adaptation Lag via Safeguarded Large Learning Rates

problem.claim: Online model selection must adapt autonomously to unknown distribution shifts while maintaining predictive accuracy in non-stationary environments.

gap.claim: Existing tuning-free algorithms trade off robustness against agility because small learning rates needed for dynamic regret guarantees cause significant adaptation lag during abrupt changes.

contributions.claim: The paper proposes an optimistic online mirror descent method using safeguarded large learning rates up to ?(T).
The method introduces a post-hoc penalty mechanism that monitors unstable updates and excludes learning rates incurring excessive regret.
The method is designed to avoid restrictive a priori learning-rate constraints while retaining near-optimal worst-case guarantees.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that cumulative penalty remains O(log T) and that the algorithm matches near-optimal worst-case guarantees while achieving superior rates in benign cases.
The authors report evaluations on three synthetic and eleven diverse real-world datasets.
The authors report reducing adaptation lag from hundreds of rounds to a few rounds and consistently outperforming tuning-free baselines.

narrative_sequence.summary: Online model selection is needed to maintain predictive accuracy under unknown distribution shifts in non-stationary environments.
Tuning-free algorithms face a robustness-agility trade-off because small learning rates create adaptation lag after abrupt changes.
The proposed approach combines optimistic online mirror descent with safeguarded large learning rates and a post-hoc penalty mechanism.
The authors state that cumulative penalty is logarithmic and that the approach preserves near-optimal worst-case guarantees while improving benign-case rates.
Evaluations across synthetic and real-world datasets are reported to show shorter adaptation lag and better performance than tuning-free baselines.

source_observation.claim: Safeguarding large learning rates with post-hoc penalties is reported to reduce adaptation lag while retaining worst-case guarantees.

interpretation.claim: Separating aggressive adaptation from stability control may help online systems respond quickly to abrupt changes.

application.claim: Online model-selection systems could consider dynamically screened large update rates when rapid adaptation is important.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish how the approach behaves outside the reported evaluation settings or under other types of distribution shift.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the exact learning-rate growth denoted by ?(T).
The abstract does not provide dataset names, baselines, evaluation protocol, or numerical performance details.
The abstract does not describe the proof assumptions or implementation details of the penalty mechanism.
